claim: Recollection refers to the retrieval process yielding memories that capture the richness of our past, including such aspects as where, when, or with whom we experienced an event.
source: Recollection refers to the retrieval process yielding memories that capture the richness of our past, including such aspects as where, when, or with whom we experienced an event (Yonelinas, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yonelinas, 2002

claim: Recollection is often accompanied by the subjective feeling of vivid remembering, a sense of mental reliving the event.
source: This process is often accompanied by the subjective feeling of vivid remembering, a sense of mental reliving the event (Tulving, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tulving, 1985

claim: At the neural level, recollection is associated with a network of brain regions including the medial temporal lobes, particularly the hippocampus and the parahippocampal gyrus, the retrosplenial/posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and the precuneus, and the medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) and the angular gyrus.
source: At the neural level, recollection is associated with a network of brain regions including the medial temporal lobes, particularly the hippocampus and the parahippocampal gyrus, the retrosplenial/posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and the precuneus, and the medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) and the angular gyrus (Rugg and Vilberg, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rugg and Vilberg, 2013

claim: The subjective sense of vivid recollection is typically positively correlated with the accuracy of recollected details.
source: The subjective sense of vivid recollection is typically positively correlated with the accuracy of recollected details (Moscovitch et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moscovitch et al., 2016

claim: The neural network underlying recollection has been reliably identified across studies that require participants either to reflect on their subjective experience or to retrieve specific memory details.
source: Indeed, the neural network underlying recollection has been reliably identified across studies that require participants either to reflect on their subjective experience (Daselaar et al., 2006; Vilberg and Rugg, 2007) or to retrieve specific memory details (Dobbins et al., 2002; Mitchell and Johnson, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Adults are more likely to correctly identify a studied item in a two alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task if the distractor corresponds to a non-studied exemplar of the target or a different section of the same scene (i.e., A-A' condition) than if the distractor corresponds to a non-studied exemplar of a different studied item (i.e., A-B' condition).
source: For example, after studying objects, faces, or parts of scenes, adults are more likely to correctly identify a studied item in a two alternative forced-choice (2AFC) task if the distractor corresponds to a non-studied exemplar of the target or a different section of the same scene (i.e., A-A' condition) than if the distractor corresponds to a non-studied exemplar of a different studied item (i.e., A-B' condition) (Dobbins et al., 1998; Heathcote et al., 2009; Hembacher and Ghetti, 2017; Tulving, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Participants are consistently less likely to claim subjective recollection in the A-A' condition.
source: However, participants are consistently less likely to claim subjective recollection in the A-A' condition, likely because it forces them to identify the most diagnostic feature from the comparison between the two perceptually similar probes.
evidence: Inference based on the experimental paradigm and cited behavioral patterns

claim: In the A-A' condition, individuals may recognize the challenge of identifying a diagnostic feature or may base their subjective recollection judgment only on that feature rather than on the entire experience.
source: Despite gaining in memory accuracy, individuals may therefore recognize the challenge of identifying a diagnostic feature or may base their subjective recollection judgment only on that feature rather than on the entire experience (Dobbins et al., 1998; Hembacher and Ghetti, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dobbins et al., 1998 and Hembacher and Ghetti, 2017

claim: Memory accuracy was higher in the A-A' than in the A-B' condition.
source: Consistent with previous studies, memory accuracy was higher in the A-A' than in the A-B' condition, estimated difference (Est.) = 0.38, SE = 0.05, p<0.0001 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2A

claim: There was a higher rate of remember responses in the A-B' than in the A-A' condition.
source: As predicted, there was an effect of experimental condition, Est. = 1.35, SE = 0.11, p<0.0001, with a higher rate of remember responses in the A-B' than in the A-A' condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The interaction between experimental condition and accuracy was significant, suggesting that although remember judgments were overall more likely in the A-B' condition, the difference as compared with the A-A' condition was more pronounced for incorrect responses.
source: The interaction between experimental condition and accuracy was also significant, Est. = −0.64, SE = 0.13, p<0.0001, suggesting that although remember judgments were overall more likely in the A-B' condition, the difference as compared with the A-A' condition was more pronounced for incorrect responses (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Remember responses were overall more likely for accurate than for inaccurate responses.
source: This interaction was found above and beyond the expected main effect of accuracy showing that remember responses were overall more likely for accurate than for inaccurate responses, Est. = 0.96, SE = 0.10, p<0.0001 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Participants were more likely to select an answer to count toward their final score in the A-B' than in the A-A' condition.
source: Participants were more likely to select an answer to count toward their final score in the A-B' than in the A-A' condition, Est. = 0.72, SE = 0.12, p<0.0001, above and beyond the greater tendency to select memories associated with remember relative to familiar judgments, Est. = 1.64, SE = 0.20, p<0.0001, and with accurate compared to inaccurate responses, Est. = 1.02, SE = 0.09, p<0.0001.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: A three-way interaction was observed between condition, rating, and accuracy.
source: Critically, we also observed a three-way interaction between condition, rating, and accuracy, Est. = −0.78, SE = 0.30, p=0.02 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2C

claim: For correct responses, selecting a response was more likely in the A-B' than in the A-A' condition.
source: For correct responses, selecting a response was more likely in the A-B' than in the A-A' condition, Est. = 0.45, SE = 0.08, p<0.0001, and more frequent for remember than for familiar judgments, Est. = 2.69, SE = 0.14, p<0.0001.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There was a significant condition by subjective judgment interaction for correct responses, such that selection rates were similar for remember ratings between conditions, but participants extended their tendency to select A-B' trials even to some familiar judgments.
source: There was also a significant condition by subjective judgment interaction, Est. = −0.64, SE = 0.18, p=0.0004, such that selection rates were similar for remember ratings between conditions, but participants extended their tendency to select A-B' trials even to some familiar judgments.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Participants showed higher drift rate estimates in the A-A' condition than in the A-B' condition.
source: An ANOVA with condition (A-A' vs. A-B') as a within-subject factor revealed significant differences in drift rate, F(1,28) = 15.48, p=0.002, ηp2 = 0.36, with higher drift rate estimates in the A-A' condition, M = 2.06, SD = 0.62, than in the A-B' condition, M = 1.22, SD = 0.61.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift diffusion model parameters

claim: Threshold separation did not differ between conditions.
source: Threshold separation, reflecting how cautious participants were in their memory choice, did not differ between conditions, F(1,28) = 3.59, p=0.07, ηp2 = 0.11 (A-A': M = 2.42, SD = 0.25; A-B': M = 2.51, SD = 0.21).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of drift diffusion model parameters

claim: Participants showed faster evidence accumulation in the A-A' than in the A-B' condition.
source: Together, evidence accumulation followed the pattern found for accuracy differences between conditions, such that participants showed faster evidence accumulation in the A-A' than in the A-B' condition, consistent with the idea that the A-A' condition promotes specific retrieval of more diagnostic features.
evidence: Inference based on drift diffusion model results

claim: The contrast A-A' > A-B' revealed greater activation in a cluster encompassing the right superior parietal lobe (SPL) and the supramarginal gyrus.
source: Consistent with our expectations, the contrast A-A' > A-B' revealed greater activation in a cluster encompassing the right superior parietal lobe (SPL) and the supramarginal gyrus (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A

claim: The contrast A-B' > A-A' revealed greater activation in the bilateral retrosplenial cortex, PCC, and the precuneus.
source: Instead, the contrast A-B' > A-A' revealed greater activation in the bilateral retrosplenial cortex, PCC, and the precuneus (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A

claim: In the SPL, there were neither differences between remember and familiar judgments, nor an interaction between subjective judgment and experimental condition.
source: In the SPL, which showed higher activation in the A-A' condition, there were neither differences between remember and familiar judgments, F(1,28) = 0.03, p=0.86, ηp2 = 0.001, nor an interaction between subjective judgment and experimental condition, F(1,28) = 0.60, p=0.45, ηp2 = 0.021 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3B

claim: In the PCC/precuneus cluster, activation was enhanced for remember relative to familiar judgments across both experimental conditions.
source: In contrast, in the PCC/precuneus cluster, which showed higher activation in the A-B' condition, activation was enhanced for remember relative to familiar judgments across both experimental conditions, F(1,28) = 30.54, p<0.001, padj < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.52 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3B

claim: There was no significant interaction between subjective judgment and experimental condition in the PCC/precuneus region.
source: We observed no significant interaction between subjective judgment and experimental condition in this region, F(1,28) = 0.02, p=0.90, padj = 0.90, ηp2 = 0.001.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: The left angular gyrus showed greater activation for remember than for familiar judgments across both experimental conditions.
source: Additional analyses comparing remember to familiar judgments in each experimental condition demonstrated that the left angular gyrus showed greater activation for remember than for familiar judgments across both experimental conditions (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The contrast between A-B' and A-A' revealed increased activation in the bilateral anterior insula, the dACC, and the right dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC).
source: The contrast between A-B' and A-A' also revealed increased activation in the bilateral anterior insula, the dACC, and the right dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC) (Figure 3A), regions that have been implicated in retrospective metacognitive assessments.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A

claim: The bilateral anterior insula showed enhanced activation for remember relative to familiar judgments across conditions.
source: The bilateral anterior insula showed enhanced activation for remember relative to familiar judgments across conditions, F(1,28) = 73.43, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.72.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: The bilateral anterior insula showed an interaction between subjective judgment and experimental condition.
source: This main effect was accompanied by an interaction with experimental condition, F(1,28) = 6.19, p=0.02, padj = 0.057, ηp2 = 0.18 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3C

claim: Anterior insula activation was similar across conditions for remember judgments, but was enhanced in the A-B' condition for familiar judgments.
source: Post hoc tests indicated that although anterior insula activation was similar across conditions for remember judgments, t(28) = 0.12, p=0.91, it was enhanced in the A-B' condition for familiar judgments, t(28) = 3.18, p=0.004.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data

claim: The cluster encompassing the dACC and dlPFC showed more pronounced engagement in remember than in familiar judgments across both experimental conditions.
source: In addition, the cluster encompassing the dACC and dlPFC showed more pronounced engagement in remember than in familiar judgments across both experimental conditions, F(1,28) = 29.49, p<0.001, padj <0.001, ηp2 = 0.51, but no interaction with condition, F(1,28) = 0.900, p=0.35, padj = 0.53, ηp2 = 0.03 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3C

claim: Hippocampal activation showed a main effect of accuracy, with enhanced activation for correct responses.
source: The results revealed a main effect of accuracy, F(1,28) = 6.39, p=0.02, ηp2 = 0.19, with enhanced activation for correct responses.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data from hippocampal ROI

claim: Hippocampal activation showed a main effect of condition with enhanced activation in the A-B' condition.
source: There was also a main effect of condition, F(1,28) = 9.17, p=0.01, ηp2 = 0.25 with enhanced activation in the A-B' condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data from hippocampal ROI

claim: There was no evidence for an accuracy-by-experimental condition interaction in the hippocampus.
source: We found no evidence for an accuracy-by-experimental condition interaction, F(1,28) = 0.04, p=0.85, ηp2 = 0.001, suggesting similar retrieval success effects across experimental conditions in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data from hippocampal ROI

claim: In the SPL, enhanced activation was observed for the A-A' compared to the A-B' condition during the decision phase.
source: In the SPL, which showed enhanced activation in the A-A' condition during the memory phase, we again observed enhanced activation for the A-A' compared to the A-B' condition during the decision phase, F(1,28) = 9.29, p=0.01, ηp2 = 0.25.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data during decision phase

claim: SPL activation was not modulated by the decision to select or discard the memory.
source: SPL activation was not modulated by the decision to select or discard the memory, F(1,28) = 0.99, p=0.33, ηp2 = 0.03, and the interaction between condition and betting decision was not significant, F(1,28) = 0.30, p=0.59, ηp2 = 0.01 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data during decision phase and shown in Figure 4A

claim: In the PCC/precuneus cluster, there was a trend for a main effect of condition with greater engagement in the A-A' condition during the decision phase.
source: In the PCC/precuneus cluster, which showed enhanced activation in the A-B' condition during the memory phase, we observed a trend for a main effect of condition with greater engagement in the A-A' condition, F(1,28) = 5.190, p=0.031, padj = 0.09, ηp2 = 0.156, no significant main effect of decision to select or discard a response, F(1,28) = 1.62, p=0.21, padj = 0.21, ηp2 = 0.06, and no decision by experimental condition interaction, F(1,28) = 0.011, p=0.92, padj = 0.92, ηp2 = 0.00 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data during decision phase and shown in Figure 4A

claim: In the bilateral anterior insula, there was a main effect of decision during the decision phase.
source: In line with this expectation, in the bilateral anterior insula, there was a main effect of decision, F(1,28) = 4.81, p=0.04, padj = 0.06, ηp2 = 0.15, along with a decision-by-confidence interaction, F(1,28) = 5.88, p=0.02, padj = 0.03, ηp2 = 0.17 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data during decision phase and shown in Figure 4B

claim: In the bilateral anterior insula, there was no main effect of experimental condition during the decision phase.
source: There was no main effect of experimental condition, F(1,28) = 0.02, p=0.90, padj = 0.90, ηp2 = 0.001.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data during decision phase

claim: In the cluster encompassing right dACC and dlPFC, there was a main effect of decision to select during the decision phase.
source: A similar pattern emerged in the cluster encompassing right dACC and dlPFC, with a main effect of decision to select, F(1,28) = 8.65, p=0.01, padj = 0.03, ηp2 = 0.236, as well as an experimental condition by decision interaction, F(1,28) = 6.09, p=0.02, padj = 0.03, ηp2 = 0.18 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data during decision phase and shown in Figure 4B

claim: In the cluster encompassing right dACC and dlPFC, there was no main effect of experimental condition during the decision phase.
source: Again, there was no main effect of experimental condition, F(1,28) = 0.07, p=0.79, padj = 0.90, ηp2 = 0.003.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data during decision phase

claim: Across all areas, activation was enhanced for decisions to discard a response, especially in the A-B' condition.
source: Across all areas, activation was enhanced for decisions to discard a response, especially in the A-B' condition (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data during decision phase and shown in Figure 4B

claim: Frontal regions showed enhanced activation for the decision to discard a memory, including bilateral middle frontal gyrus extending into the bilateral frontal pole, and the right angular gyrus.
source: In analogy to the ROI results above, frontal regions showed enhanced activation for the decision to discard a memory, including bilateral middle frontal gyrus extending into the bilateral frontal pole, and the right angular gyrus (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis during decision phase and shown in Figure 4C

claim: The decision to select a response was associated with increased activation in ventral temporal areas and posterior hippocampus.
source: In contrast, the decision to select a response was associated with increased activation in ventral temporal areas and posterior hippocampus (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis during decision phase and shown in Figure 4C

claim: When participants encountered a target studied item along with a perceptually similar lure, their memory accuracy was higher, but their subjective recollection was lower (A-A' condition) compared to when participants encountered a target studied item along with a lure that was similar to another studied item (A-B' condition).
source: When participants encountered a target studied item along with a perceptually similar (and semantically identical) lure, their memory accuracy was higher, but their subjective recollection was lower (A-A' condition) compared to when participants encountered a target studied item along with a lure that was similar to another studied item (A-B' condition).
evidence: Summary of behavioral findings from the study

claim: The A-A' condition was associated with enhanced activation in the right SPL across both remember and familiar responses.
source: Specifically, the A-A' condition was associated with enhanced activation in the right SPL across both remember and familiar responses.
evidence: Summary of fMRI findings from the study

claim: The A-B' condition was associated with enhanced activation in the bilateral precuneus and retrosplenial cortex, which also showed overall greater engagement during remember than during familiar responses in both experimental conditions.
source: In contrast, the A-B' condition was associated with enhanced activation in the bilateral precuneus and retrosplenial cortex, which also showed overall greater engagement during remember than during familiar responses in both experimental conditions.
evidence: Summary of fMRI findings from the study

claim: When the retrieval context favors identifying more precise diagnostic features, the resulting higher accuracy is associated with dorsal PPC at the expense of subjective recollection.
source: Together, these findings suggest that when the retrieval context favors identifying more precise diagnostic features, the resulting higher accuracy is associated with dorsal PPC at the expense of subjective recollection.
evidence: Inference based on the pattern of fMRI and behavioral results

claim: Activation in the precuneus and retrosplenial cortex tracks the experience of subjective recollection, which is promoted in a retrieval context that favors global retrieval.
source: In contrast, activation in the precuneus and retrosplenial cortex tracks the experience of subjective recollection, which is promoted in a retrieval context that favors global retrieval.
evidence: Inference based on the pattern of fMRI and behavioral results

claim: Regions of the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) have been associated with retrieval of accurate details as well as with subjective recollection.
source: Regions of the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) have been associated with retrieval of accurate details (Wagner et al., 2005) as well as with subjective recollection (Chua et al., 2006; Simons et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research

claim: High-performing older adults showed similar levels of subjective recollection to younger adults but lower levels of objective recollection.
source: High-performing older adults showed similar levels of subjective recollection to younger adults but lower levels of objective recollection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Duarte et al., 2008

claim: While older adults displayed significantly lower objective memory, there were no age differences in subjective recollection.
source: While older adults displayed significantly lower objective memory, there were no age differences in subjective recollection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mark and Rugg, 1998

claim: Frithsen and Miller, 2014 showed enhanced activation in the angular gyrus in association with subjective recollection.
source: In a direct comparison of subjective (remember-know procedure) and objective recollection (source memory test), Frithsen and Miller, 2014 showed enhanced activation in the angular gyrus in association with subjective recollection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Frithsen and Miller, 2014

claim: Richter et al., 2016 reported that activation in the angular gyrus was associated with objective memory precision, whereas activation in the precuneus was associated with subjective memory vividness.
source: Further dissociating the precision of memory retrieval from memory vividness, Richter et al., 2016 reported that activation in the angular gyrus was associated with objective memory precision, whereas activation in the precuneus was associated with subjective memory vividness.
evidence: Supported by citation to Richter et al., 2016

claim: Memory goals biased feature representation toward relevant information in dorsal PPC but not in ventral PPC.
source: The results demonstrated that memory goals biased feature representation toward relevant information in dorsal PPC but not in ventral PPC.
evidence: Supported by citation to Favila et al., 2018

claim: Metacognitive assessments of decision confidence have been associated with activation in dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and anterior insula supporting performance or error monitoring.
source: Metacognitive assessments of decision confidence, which represent retrospective metacognitive monitoring, have been associated with activation in dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and anterior insula supporting performance or error monitoring (Fandakova et al., 2018), and with activation in lateral PFC to support the evaluation of retrieved content in the context of current task demands (Bang and Fleming, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fandakova et al., 2018 and Bang and Fleming, 2018

claim: Participants were more likely to bet on their responses in the A-B' condition in anticipation of a social reward.
source: Interestingly, a behavioral study found that participants were more likely to bet on their responses in the A-B' condition in anticipation of a social reward (Hembacher and Ghetti, 2017), suggesting that cues utilized to support subjective recollection are more heavily factored in subsequent decision making than cues associated with accurate response selection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hembacher and Ghetti, 2017

claim: The A-A' condition was associated with higher rates of evidence accumulation.
source: Consistent with this, we found that the A-A' condition was associated with higher rates of evidence accumulation.
evidence: Supported by drift diffusion model analysis of experimental data

claim: The SPL plays an important role in supporting diagnostic processing during retrieval.
source: Together, our behavioral and neural results converge to suggest that the SPL plays an important role in supporting diagnostic processing during retrieval.
evidence: Inference based on combined behavioral and fMRI results

claim: The SPL has an established role in the dorsal attention network.
source: These findings are in line with the established role of the SPL in the dorsal attention network (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002) and corroborate a recent suggestion that this region supports higher memory accuracy via its role in perceptual search and attention to probes during retrieval (Sestieri et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corbetta and Shulman, 2002 and Sestieri et al., 2017

claim: The precuneus has been implicated consistently in autobiographical retrieval.
source: The precuneus has been implicated consistently in autobiographical retrieval (McDermott et al., 2009) and may be one of the distinguishing features of individuals with superior memory (Mazzoni et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to McDermott et al., 2009 and Mazzoni et al., 2019

claim: Memory for recently learned scenes was associated with activation of the posterior middle intraparietal sulcus, while autobiographical memories involving scenes engaged the retrosplenial cortex and the precuneus.
source: A recent study compared retrieval of recently studied events and autobiographical events (Chen et al., 2017) and found that while memory for recently learned scenes was associated with activation of the posterior middle intraparietal sulcus, autobiographical memories involving scenes engaged the retrosplenial cortex and the precuneus.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2017

claim: The anterior insula may signal salient information during retrieval in light of concurrent goals.
source: Specifically, the anterior insula may signal salient information during retrieval in light of concurrent goals (Craig, 2009; Fandakova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Craig, 2009 and Fandakova et al., 2018

claim: The anterior insula and dACC have been implicated in retrospective metacognitive monitoring.
source: In separate literature on metacognition, the anterior insula as well as the dACC have been implicated in retrospective metacognitive monitoring (Fleck et al., 2006; Morales et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fleck et al., 2006 and Morales et al., 2018

claim: Lateral PFC regions have been implicated in the evaluation of retrieval outputs in context of current goals and demands.
source: Furthermore, lateral PFC regions have been implicated in the evaluation of retrieval outputs in context of current goals and demands (Chua et al., 2006; Fandakova et al., 2014; Kim and Cabeza, 2009), and in making decisions based on retrieved output (Fandakova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Fandakova et al., 2018 showed that the anterior insula and dACC were activated both when participants inaccurately remembered the context in which an object was encountered as well as when they decided to withhold their reports of memory for item–context associations.
source: For example, Fandakova et al., 2018 showed that the anterior insula and dACC were activated both when participants inaccurately remembered the context in which an object was encountered as well as when they decided to withhold their reports of memory for item–context associations, whereas the anterior PFC was uniquely engaged when participants withheld an answer.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fandakova et al., 2018

claim: Hippocampus activation distinguished between successful vs. unsuccessful retrieval but did not vary with memory precision or subjective vividness.
source: These results are consistent with a previous study by Richter et al., 2016 who found that hippocampus activation distinguished between successful vs. unsuccessful retrieval but did not vary with memory precision or subjective vividness.
evidence: Supported by citation to Richter et al., 2016

claim: While hippocampus plays a key role for episodic memory, it is not the main driver of the subjective experience of recollection and is less dependent on the specific context in which retrieval takes place.
source: These results tentatively suggest that while hippocampus plays a key role for episodic memory, it is not the main driver of the subjective experience of recollection and is less dependent on the specific context in which retrieval takes place.
evidence: Inference based on hippocampal findings in the study

claim: Activation in the retrosplenia cortex and the precuneus was associated with subjective recollection when participants retrieved item-relevant information and they did not have to compare opposing mnemonic signals regarding their diagnostic value.
source: In contrast, activation in the retrosplenia cortex and the precuneus was associated with subjective recollection when participants retrieved item-relevant information and they did not have to compare opposing mnemonic signals regarding their diagnostic value.
evidence: Summary and interpretation of fMRI findings

claim: Insular, cingulate, and lateral frontal regions signal saliency of the retrieved information at retrieval, which will then be carried over to later decision stages where these task-relevant signals are recapitulated and evaluated in the context of concurrent goals.
source: In line with the nature of subjective recollection judgments as metacognitive assessments that guide upcoming decision making, insular, cingulate, and lateral frontal regions signal saliency of the retrieved information at retrieval. This will then be carried over to later decision stages where these task-relevant signals are recapitulated and evaluated in the context of concurrent goals.
evidence: Summary and interpretation of fMRI findings across memory and decision phases

claim: Thirty healthy right-handed volunteers (18–25 years, M = 21.0, SD = 1.7, 15 females) with no history of or current neurological or psychiatric illness participated in the study.
source: Thirty healthy right-handed volunteers (18–25 years, M = 21.0, SD = 1.7, 15 females) with no history of or current neurological or psychiatric illness participated in the study after signing informed consent approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of California, Davis (protocol #217322).
evidence: Description of study participants

claim: One additional participant took part in the experiment but was excluded from further analyses due to an incidental finding.
source: One additional participant took part in the experiment but was excluded from further analyses due to an incidental finding.
evidence: Description of participant exclusion

claim: One participant failed to comply with instructions, resulting in a final sample of 29 participants included in the present analyses.
source: One participant failed to comply with instructions, resulting in a final sample of 29 participants included in the present analyses.
evidence: Description of participant exclusion

claim: Stimuli included pairs of 342 color images of familiar everyday objects.
source: Stimuli included pairs of 342 color images of familiar everyday objects.
evidence: Description of experimental stimuli

claim: During the encoding task, participants were presented with 342 unique items across three runs (114 items per run).
source: During the encoding task, participants were presented with 342 unique items across three runs (114 items per run).
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: Participants viewed each object for 1500 ms while performing an indoor–outdoor judgment.
source: Participants viewed each object for 1500 ms while performing an indoor–outdoor judgment.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: The retrieval task included a total of 228 2AFC recognition trials distributed across three runs with 76 trials per run.
source: The retrieval task included a total of 228 2AFC recognition trials distributed across three runs with 76 trials per run.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: In each run, there were a total of 38 A-A' trials in which the lure depicted a different version of the same object and 38 A-B' trials in which the lure depicted a different version of a studied object that was not concurrently presented on the screen.
source: In each run, there were a total of 38 A-A' trials in which the lure depicted a different version of the same object (Figure 1B) and 38 A-B' trials in which the lure depicted a different version of a studied object that was not concurrently presented on the screen (and was not used as a target in other trials).
evidence: Description of experimental procedure shown in Figure 1B

claim: Participants were instructed to select about 50% of the trials.
source: Participants were instructed to select about 50% of the trials.
evidence: Description of experimental instructions

claim: Participants were told that their final score would be ranked in comparison to all other students who had participated in the study, and their ranking would be displayed on the screen at the end of the task in the presence of the experimenter.
source: To motivate participants, they were told that their final score would be ranked in comparison to all other students who had participated in the study, and their ranking would be displayed on the screen at the end of the task in the presence of the experimenter.
evidence: Description of experimental motivation procedure

claim: At the end of the task, participants were debriefed that the ranking did not exist.
source: At the end of the task, participants were debriefed that the ranking did not exist.
